▌National Sheriffs' Association Withdraws Opposition to the CLARITY Act, Becoming Neutral

On September 5th, the National Sheriffs' Association (NSA) announced that it was withdrawing its opposition to the CLARITY Act, the cryptocurrency market structure bill, and becoming "neutral." In a letter to Senate Majority Leader John Thune and Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, the NSA stated that given the extensive work already done by Congress, the government, and industry stakeholders on the legal, regulatory, and enforcement issues addressed by the bill, the organization decided to "step back and allow the legislative process to continue" to establish a clear, effective, and urgently needed regulatory framework.

Previously, the NSA opposed certain provisions in the bill concerning regulatory exemptions for cryptocurrency mixers, arguing that such provisions could weaken law enforcement's ability to track on-chain transactions and recover victims' funds. The NSA also criticized the CLARITY Act for "protecting the crypto industry, not the public." Currently, the US Senate plans to proceed with a procedural vote on the CLARITY Act on September 15. While the bill has made progress with the Senate Agriculture and Banking Committees, issues such as stablecoin rewards, tokenized stocks, and potential conflicts of interest with the Trump family remain controversial.

Oakville, Ontario, and Rockieville, Alberta, have suspended data center projects for a year, and Manitoba Premier Wabue Keeneau also rejected a data center construction plan near Winnipeg. Some residents are concerned about the high power consumption and noise levels of large data centers, and the potential for driving up electricity prices. Canada currently has five large data centers in operation, with another 159 projects announced or under construction. ZeroBytes had previously claimed to have sold some of the stolen tax data to buyers. Recently, fake DGFiP paper mail targeting Crypto holders has also appeared in France. Scammers use the pretext of DAC8 digital asset declaration to lure recipients into scanning QR codes to phishing websites and steal wallet information. ▌Can Bitcoin Still Be Called "Digital Gold" During Geopolitical Crises?

Every geopolitical crisis causes gold prices to rise while Bitcoin prices plummet. After six tests, the claim of "digital gold" has never been supported by data. Countries hoard gold but exclude Bitcoin from their reserves. For investors, Bitcoin exhibits asymmetry: it falls with stocks but does not rise with them. Three structural asymmetries prevent Bitcoin from achieving safe-haven status: an oversupply of derivatives (market structure), the dominance of leveraged traders (participant composition), and a lack of repeatable behavioral records (behavioral accumulation).

Bitcoin is not a safe-haven asset, but it is a "crisis-useful asset," which can indeed function when borders are closed and banks fail. If these three asymmetries are reduced, Bitcoin may no longer be a replica of gold but rather a completely new "next-generation gold."

Generational shifts and the widespread application of algorithms are key factors that could accelerate this process.

data.title: Fomo earns 1.2 million a day, so why are the two major exchanges nervous?
data.description: On September 3rd, data from on-chain data agency SolanaFloor showed that social trading app Fomo's daily revenue reached $1.2 million, setting a new record. While this figure doesn't rank in the top five within the entire crypto industry, what unsettles the wallet teams at Binance and OKX isn't the number itself, but rather the underlying logic that even these two established exchanges failed to replicate. What's truly interesting is that Fomo itself doesn't shy away from the fact that its products have shortcomings, even the founders don't deny them. In an interview, co-founder Se Yong Park frankly admitted that the web version of Fomo is "a bit lacking in functionality," remaining at the level it was at launch, and the team currently doesn't have the resources to polish it—but web version traffic already accounts for about 25% of the platform's total traffic, an entry point that even the team admits is "lacking in quality." However, this hasn't stopped it from surging along its growth curve. According to data from Dune Analytics, Fomo's trading bot has achieved the number one position in trading volume and market share in the meme trading sector; Se Yong revealed in an interview that the platform's users have grown to 1.3 million, and are still adding 30,000 net users every day. Looking back, according to statistics from the on-chain data platform DeFiLlama, Fomo set a record of $2.64 million in protocol revenue for a single week on August 8th, breaking its own weekly revenue record three times within a month, with annualized revenue reaching $29.22 million at one point; on August 16th, its single-day protocol revenue even surpassed that of the established derivatives platform Hyperliquid; on August 21st, Fomo briefly entered the top three of the US financial application rankings, surpassing Cash App and the prediction market Kalshi, and is currently stable within the top 15. Behind this is a $75 million Series B funding round led by Silicon Valley veteran Index Ventures, with participation from established venture capital firm Union Square Ventures (USV). This round valued the company, founded by three former employees of the decentralized exchange dYdX, at $550 million, bringing its total disclosed equity funding to approximately $94 million. What truly worries Binance and OKX isn't user volume, but rather the workflow Fomo has established: information flow → trading → creator revenue sharing. When a user buys a token on Fomo, they can casually write a short "why they bought it" thesis. If someone sees this purchase record and follows suit, the original author receives a portion of the transaction fees generated (Creator Revenue). According to co-founder Se Yong Park, the Trader Rewards program alone disbursed nearly $2 million in a single week at the end of August. This means that even a regular account with only a few hundred followers can earn a share of this money if their trades are copied, without having to accumulate tens of thousands of followers, accept advertisements, or do rebates as in the past. What are Binance and OKX in such a hurry for? According to KOL CryptoBraveHQ (@cryptobraveHQ), OKX has held multiple internal meetings, hoping to replicate Fomo's functionality in its own wallet. He also believes that exchange wallets developed by Chinese teams generally lack a natural understanding of overseas "leading" communities and the original culture of Western memes, a gap that cannot be bridged with a single product iteration. Binance, on the other hand, has absolutely no intention of following Fomo's approach. It's sticking to its strongest strategy—first, attract users by creating a profit-making effect through assets, then addressing product experience gaps later. On September 2nd, Binance Alpha just added the meme coin, FLORD. According to our observations, this coin quickly gained popularity within days of its launch, a perfect example of Binance's consistent approach on BNB Chain—first create a profit story to attract attention, then address the technology and product development later. This is also the most crucial point of contention in this competition: Binance and OKX hold the moat of the right to issue assets—the power to decide which assets are seen first; while Fomo is leveraging the power of information—the power to be closest to the trading decision. For the past decade, exchanges have been able to capture the vast majority of trading volume simply by leveraging the former, because on-chain information is scattered across countless Telegram groups and X (formerly Twitter) KOLs, and exchanges don't need to consolidate it. Now, Fomo packages these scattered information flows, real positions, and revenue sharing mechanisms into a single product, essentially bypassing the issuance of rights and directly building a new entry point in the "attention-trading" link. It's worth noting that this competition is unlikely to simply boil down to a choice between "Fomo or exchange wallets." Another slightly different approach in the market comes from Coinbase's Base ecosystem—it doesn't compete on meme culture or create wealth through asset issuance, but instead focuses on making wallets compliant payments, fiat currency gateways, and on-chain financial infrastructure. In other words, the wallet race is shifting from a single competition of "who has the most comprehensive functions" to several parallel moats of "who controls the culture, who controls the assets, and who controls the compliant infrastructure." The battle between exchange wallets and Fomo is just one of the most direct lines of attack. It's not just exchanges that are anxious. This battle for trading gateways isn't limited to Binance and OKX alone. According to Se Yong Park in an interview, just a week before this interview, Pump.fun, a long-established meme coin launch platform, was reported to be poaching top traders from the Fomo platform with hefty sums. In Fomo's model, a trader's personal account is itself an asset; whoever's positions are seen and followed by more people receives a larger share of the creator's revenue, making top traders a scarce resource that various platforms are vying for. Se Yong's response to this was quite restrained: competition is a good thing; Fomo's goal is to expand the entire "pie," rather than confining itself to the existing crypto Twitter (CT) circle to grab users. According to him, Fomo doesn't even want to define itself as a "crypto company," but rather wants to become a social financial platform where "anything can be traded." This statement sounds like public relations rhetoric, but considering its already planned community feature (Clans)—where users can team up to participate in leaderboard battles, co-build funding pools, and even receive airdrops from projects under the community name—it's clear that Fomo isn't just targeting Binance and OKX wallet users, but also the top traders held by platforms like Pump.fun. The previous revenue-sharing model, which directly linked "trading recommendations" to trading volume for profit sharing, wasn't invented by Fomo. The established social trading platform eToro's Popular Investor program adopted a similar logic years ago: bloggers' monthly income is linked to their AUC (Amount Under Traded), with higher tiers receiving a larger share. This mechanism has indeed cultivated a group of top trading bloggers, but it has also been accompanied by long-standing controversy—when income is directly tied to "how many people follow their trades," do bloggers have an incentive to increase their positions and create more sensational narratives to attract more followers? This question has been debated for over a decade with eToro: should the upper limit of a single blogger's share be limited, or should the market be allowed to weed out those who fail? There is still no unified approach in the industry. Fomo's trader rewards and creator revenue sharing essentially bring the same incentive structure onto the blockchain and into the already highly volatile MIME coin market. The leaderboards and feeds create verifiable public records of bloggers' positions and profits/losses, making them harder to fake than DEX leaderboards which are easily manipulated. However, this same mechanism could also distort the "sharing trading logic" into "creating trading signals for revenue sharing." This isn't a problem Binance or OKX currently needs to worry about, but it's a question every ordinary user preparing to invest in the Fomo ecosystem should consider carefully. Fomo has not yet confirmed whether it will issue a token. A platform that just secured $75 million, is aggressively subsidizing traders and creators, has been poached by Pump.fun, and is being studied and copied by OKX—will it refine its revenue-sharing mechanism into a more transparent information pricing method, or will the pressure to grow cause "market recommendation equals profit" to "market recommendation equals manipulation"? No one can say for sure. And this answer will ultimately determine not only the valuation of an app, but also who should define the next generation of trading gateways—will it continue to be determined by exchanges through issuance rights, or will it be defined by countless ordinary users using their own positions and theses?

data.title: No longer just talking about APR: After staking, whose ETH do you actually own?
data.description:
After staking 32 ETH into a validator, does that money still belong to "yours"? In today's market saturated with various staking products, this is a seemingly basic question that is often overlooked. In the past, when choosing a staking plan, people would meticulously compare: Which company offers a 0.2% higher APR? Is the transaction fee 5% or 10%? Does it automatically compound interest? When can I get a refund? However, with the benchmark staking yield across the entire network now flattened to below 3%, the slight differences in paper yields between different platforms are no longer significant. Compared to fussing over a few thousandths of an interest rate, another question, often hidden beneath the product interface, is far more important: Who controls your ETH after you stake it? I. The Underlying Logic of Staking: The Doer Can't Manage the Money. To understand non-custodial staking, the key is to grasp a very ingenious design Ethereum employs at the consensus layer. Running a validator is never just about a single key; it splits permissions into two distinct halves at the protocol level. One type is the Signing Key, which is the private key for verifying signatures. This key is specifically used for "working," participating in Attestation, proposing blocks, and completing various consensus tasks 24/7. It must be directly connected to the server and always online. Whoever holds this key is responsible for running that machine. However, it can only be used to prove that you are honestly doing consensus. Even if you use this key to sign 10,000 times, you can never use the principal. Moreover, if the machine goes offline or even commits a double signature violation, Ethereum will deduct the validator's earnings or principal. The other type is Withdrawal Credentials, which are the withdrawal control rights pointed to by the withdrawal certificate. This is the true "withdrawal key," hardcoded into the Beacon Chain the moment the staking takes effect, determining where the staked ETH and its generated returns can ultimately be withdrawn. This key can quietly reside in your cold wallet or mnemonic phrase, never needing an internet connection. In fact, Ethereum's official positioning of the two is very clear: **Verification signature keys are "hot" permissions that require being online, while withdrawal certificates represent "cold" permissions at the level of fund ownership.** This means that a third party can run a validator for a user without necessarily owning the user's ETH. This is why non-custodial staking like imToken works—node service providers (such as InfStones) hold the Signing Key, responsible for data center operations, network attack prevention, and 24/7 online availability. It determines how smoothly the node runs and how much block reward it earns, but even after searching through the code, you won't find a single line of instruction to withdraw staked funds to themselves. Even after Ethereum upgraded and introduced EIP-7002 (Execution Layer Triggerable Exit), this closed loop of control became even more extreme. Previously, if a node operator went missing or reneged on their promise, while they couldn't take the money, users wanting to leave the validator often had to wait for the operator to broadcast a withdrawal message using the Signing Key, leaving them in a passive position. However, with EIP-7002, as long as you have the withdrawal certificate (0x01 / 0x02), you can use your imToken wallet to directly issue a command at the execution layer to forcibly shut down the validator and queue for refunds. In other words, even if the node service provider completely disappears one day, your money won't be stuck on the chain. This is precisely the point of concern regarding "non-custodial" systems: while a third party participates in the entire staking process, those responsible for the work don't simultaneously have the right to take the money. II. What can users, wallets, node service providers, and Ethereum actually do?

Continuing to break down this line, we find that a seemingly simple ETH staking actually involves at least four roles.

These are the user, the wallet, the node service provider, and the Ethereum protocol itself, although their permissions differ.

First, the user.

In a true non-custodial architecture, the user retains the most crucial control over their funds.

Taking imToken's non-custodial ETH staking as an example, the user has withdrawal permissions, and the service provider cannot arbitrarily transfer staked assets to their own account. Validator status can also be directly queried on-chain.

This is fundamentally different from what many people usually understand as "entrusting your cryptocurrency to someone else for management." While ETH is no longer in the user's wallet balance but has entered the Ethereum Deposit Contract and become a validator's balance, it hasn't become the asset of the relevant nodes. Nodes maintain the Validator for you, controlling its working permissions, not the right to withdraw assets. Secondly, there's the wallet. The wallet is more like an entry point for users to manage these permissions, not the owner of the staked assets. It helps users initiate staking, manage addresses, sign operations, and view validator status and rewards, but as long as the underlying design still adheres to non-custodial principles, the wallet service provider itself does not automatically gain the right to withdraw user assets simply by providing this interface. Therefore, "staking through a wallet" and "custodying ETH with this wallet" are actually two completely different concepts. What truly determines the nature of the transaction is still how the underlying Key and Withdrawal Credentials are configured. The third role is the node service provider. This is the most easily misunderstood aspect of non-custodial staking. Since users don't have machines running 24/7, validators must be maintained. The node service provider is responsible for running the client, keeping it online, completing validation tasks, and storing the Signing Key used for these tasks. This means they remain crucial; frequent downtime will cause users to lose some of their expected rewards, and serious violations will pose a slashing risk. Therefore, "non-custodial" never means "no service provider risk." This risk is primarily limited to the quality and profitability of the validator's operation, rather than whether the service provider can transfer your 32 ETH. The final element is the Ethereum protocol itself. This layer is often the most easily overlooked. Once ETH enters a validator, no party can transfer it whenever they want, like a regular wallet balance. It must adhere to Ethereum's unified rules, such as when it can be activated, when it can be deactivated, whether deactivation requires queuing, what actions by the validator will result in penalties, and when the withdrawal will ultimately be completed—all determined by the protocol. The same applies to Pectra's 0x02 Compounding Validator, which increases the validator's effective balance from the traditional 32 ETH cap to a maximum of 2048 ETH, allowing rewards to continue compounding, but withdrawals and exits still follow the protocol. Third, what about Lido? What is sacrificed behind liquidity? Once this framework is established, the difference becomes very clear when looking at liquidity staking like Lido. After a user deposits ETH into Lido, they receive stETH, and stETH itself still belongs entirely to the user; it can be transferred, traded, or used in DeFi. This is also the greatest value of Liquid Staking, allowing liquidity that was originally locked in Validators to be released back into the system. However, at the same time, the underlying ETH control structure has also changed. Lido aggregates the ETH held by a large number of users and then distributes it to different Node Operators to create and operate validators. The Withdrawal Credentials of these validators are not the individual Ethereum addresses of each stETH user, but are uniformly set by the Lido protocol. The underlying withdrawal process is also jointly completed by the protocol's smart contracts, Oracle, node operators, and other components. Therefore, users hold staking rights represented by stETH, not Withdrawal Credentials belonging solely to a particular Validator. When a user wants to redeem ETH from the protocol, they need to submit stETH to the Lido Withdrawal Queue, wait for the protocol to complete the corresponding exit and fund preparation, and then claim the ETH. Lido will generate an NFT representing the withdrawal right for this withdrawal request, and the user can only claim the underlying ETH after the request is completed. However, although it appears that the user still holds stETH, and the protocol itself operates through smart contracts, meaning there is no centralized institution that can arbitrarily take all user assets, it does have a different trust boundary than native staking where each user has one validator and the withdrawal address directly belongs to the user. The former results in a lower barrier to entry, better liquidity, and stETH's extensive composability in DeFi; the latter sacrifices some liquidity and requires at least 32 ETH, but makes the fund control relationship of the underlying validator more direct. In simple terms, Liquid Staking is more like holding a freely tradable "staking asset certificate," while non-custodial native staking is closer to having your own validator, only outsourcing its daily operations. Neither is inherently superior. For users with only a few ETH who need to trade frequently or want to participate in DeFi, liquid staking assets like stETH are clearly more convenient. However, if a user holds 32 ETH, 64 ETH, or even more for an extended period and doesn't have a strong need for liquidity, the yield difference might not be significant enough to determine their choice. In this case, the security consideration of "who controls the assets" becomes far more important. After all, staking yields change daily; the APR (Average Revenue Per Second) fluctuates with the total amount staked across the network, and fees may also adjust. Ultimately, where Withdrawal Credentials point, who can withdraw the principal, and whether third-party cooperation is needed in extreme situations determine the fundamental trust structure of the entire product. This might be an easily overlooked change as ETH staking matures: As the returns and experiences of various products become increasingly similar, the real difference will likely stem from a fundamental question—who ultimately controls my ETH? In conclusion, there is no absolute right or wrong choice. If you only have two or three ETH, or are keen on playing the revolving lending game in DeFi, then from both a capital utilization and barrier-of-entry perspective, liquidity staking tokens like stETH are a more pragmatic choice. However, if your goal is to build a core holding in the Ethereum network over the medium to long term, whether it's 32 or more, the situation changes completely. When the net yield difference between various products is only a few thousandths or even a few basis points, taking on lengthy contract calls and governance risks for such a small return is extremely low cost-effectiveness. In the crypto industry, people often say, "Not your keys, not your coins." But in the context of staking, perhaps it should also include an additional clause: "Not your withdrawal credentials, not your native stake."

Author: BITWU.ETH Source: X, @Bitwux

Today, Robinhood Chain's issuance platform, Long.xyz, launched a pairing feature with NVIDIA tokens at 3x leverage; Robinhood Chain has become a major battleground for memes, with $PONS, $AI, and $BONER all hitting all-time highs, often seeing dozens of times the increase in a week. It's that time of year again when many people are rapidly accumulating wealth.

Below, I've broken down this sector from the perspectives of underlying assets, trading mechanisms, recent data, and participation opportunities to see where the opportunities lie.

First, let's define a basic concept:

The Meme is not "buying a Meme is the same as buying stocks," but rather it transforms stock tokens into the Meme's pricing currency, liquid asset, and narrative collateral.

Its truly valuable innovation is that, for the first time, stock tokens are not just used to "track US stock prices," but rather, like ETH, SOL, and USDC, they are placed in trading pools, lending protocols, vaults, and derivatives, becoming on-chain basic financial assets.

Essentially, it's still a continuation of DeFi.

What is actually happening now is: Meme popularity → Increased demand for stock tokens → A large number of stock tokens are locked in the Meme pool → Liquidity in the ordinary stock token pool thins → On-chain packaged asset prices are temporarily distorted → Authorized participants issue more stock tokens to restore prices. What hasn't actually happened yet is: Meme buying → Large-scale buying of real US stocks → Squeezing Wall Street short sellers → Real stock prices surge. There's still a difference of several orders of magnitude between the two. II. What exactly is a Crypto-Stock Meme? "Crypto-Stock Meme" isn't a strictly official term; I prefer to define it as: a Meme that uses stock tokens as the pricing asset, liquidity asset, transaction fee asset, or vault asset. To understand it, you must first separate the following four layers. The first layer: Robinhood Chain. Robinhood Chain is the public blockchain mainnet launched by Robinhood on July 1, 2026. Essentially, it's a Layer 2 blockchain based on Arbitrum technology, settled on Ethereum, and using ETH to pay gas. Its Chain ID is 4663. Robinhood positions itself as a financial services platform and the RWA public blockchain, supporting stock tokens, lending, staking, trading, and derivatives. The second layer consists of Robinhood Stock Tokens (HIMS, NVDA, TSLA, AAPL). These are not actual company stocks, but rather tokenized debt securities issued by Robinhood Assets (Jersey) Limited. They are pledged 1:1 against the underlying stock according to official rules, but holders do not directly own company equity, voting rights, or shareholder rights; they only gain economic exposure to the underlying securities. Ordinary users primarily buy and sell through the secondary market; the direct minting and burning in the primary market are mainly handled by authorized participants or market makers. Therefore: Holding NVDA Stock Tokens is not equivalent to holding Nvidia stock in a US brokerage account; it is an on-chain security product issued by RHJ, backed by real stock, and tracking the economic value of Nvidia; users simultaneously bear the risks of the issuer, custody, smart contracts, chain, oracle, and liquidity. The third layer: Meme Tokens. BONER, AI, microduck, and SAYLORMOON are another set of independent ERC-20 tokens. They may be associated with stocks like HIMS, NVDA, and MSTR, but holding these memes: does not represent holding the corresponding Stock Tokens; does not represent owning real stock; and usually cannot be exchanged for stock tokens at a fixed ratio.

Fourth Layer: Meme / Stock Token Liquidity Pool

What truly connects the two is the AMM trading pool.

Without stock assets or protocol revenue, primarily trading Robinhood Chain's attention, community consensus, and new chain beta.

2. Stock-paired Memes

Representatives:

  • AI/NVDA;

  • BONER/HIMS;

  • microduck/NVDA;

  • SAYLORMOON/MSTR;

  • SHRUB/TSLA.

This is the most typical "crypto-stock meme".

Stock tokens are priced and liquid assets, but they do not provide a fixed floor for the value of a meme.

3. Stock Vault or Transaction Tax-Type Memes

For example, some projects levy taxes on meme transactions and then use the transaction fees to purchase Stock Tokens such as NVDA, AAPL, and MSFT, placing them in a community vault or distributing them to specific holders.

... These projects may resemble on-chain ETFs, but they are fundamentally different: They typically lack standardized creation and redemption; Meme Tokens do not necessarily represent legal ownership of the vault; Vault growth depends on Meme's own continuous trading volume; and once the hype dies down, the cash flow from purchasing stock tokens will also decrease. Similar to The Index's design, which charges fees for transactions and purchases a basket of stock tokens, it cannot be simply understood as a traditional redeemable index fund. 4. Launch Platform and Selling Shovel Assets Representative: PONS. PONS is not a pure meme; it represents the launch platform, trading volume, transaction fee revenue, and expected buyback and burn. As of August 31, Pons had launched approximately 389,000 tokens, accounting for nearly 80% of the platform's trading volume at one point; cumulative user fees were approximately $46.06 million, protocol revenue was approximately $10.14 million, and approximately $3.61 million was used for buybacks and burns. In the last 30 days, protocol revenue was approximately $5.2 million, and buybacks and burns totaled approximately $1.62 million. However, it's important to note: Buybacks and burns do not equate to holders receiving cash dividends. Recent earnings are also in a period of extreme Meme frenzy and cannot be mechanically annualized. As of September 1st, PONS' market capitalization was approximately $294 million, up about 361% in the past seven days, with a 24-hour trading volume of approximately $106 million. Mechanically annualizing the recent 30-day earnings would superficially appear to be about 4.7 times the "annualized protocol earnings," but this valuation is only meaningful if current earnings are sustainable. 5. Leveraged Positions Tokenized The LongX NVDA3X shown in the screenshot is not a regular Stock Token. It packages a 3x NVDA leveraged exposure based on the Lighter liquidity engine into an ERC-20 that can be directly held and transferred, with position management and rebalancing handled by the protocol. It's closer to: "an on-chain, automatically managed 3x leveraged ETP," rather than 3x collateralized Nvidia stock. Risks include: perpetual contract funding rates; automatic rebalancing; volatility attenuation and path dependence; liquidation or underlying position management risks; oracle and smart contract risks; and third-party protocol risks associated with Lighter and LongX. Using NVDA3X to create a Meme is equivalent to: Meme volatility × stock volatility × 3x leverage × liquidity risk. This is the riskiest category in the entire sector and should not be treated as a regular NVDA token. Robinhood has also explicitly stated that third-party projects appearing on its ecosystem page do not represent Robinhood's endorsement of their security, legality, or suitability. VII. Just how hot is the market right now? As of September 1, 2026, Robinhood Chain's: DeFi TVL was approximately $723 million; Stablecoin size was approximately $797 million; RWA Active Market Cap was approximately $164 million; 24-hour DEX trading volume was approximately $1.403 billion; 24-hour application fees were approximately $14.4 million; 24-hour application revenue was approximately $3.01 million. Bridged TVL is approximately $2.381 billion. CoinGecko's statistics show that the market capitalization of Robinhood Chain's native meme sector is approximately $535 million, with a 24-hour trading volume of approximately $119 million. This classification does not necessarily include PONS categorized as Launchpad, nor does it fully cover all stock-paired memes; therefore, the "total ecosystem market capitalization" of different platforms cannot be directly added together. These data from CoinGecko illustrate two points: First, Robinhood Chain is no longer a new chain without funding; its stablecoins, TVL, and trading volume have all reached a considerable scale. Second, current activity is highly dependent on memes, launch platforms, and trading bots. Huge trading volume does not equate to an equivalent net inflow, as it may include high-frequency turnover, bot trading, arbitrage, and duplicate trading. VIII. Which projects are most worth researching? Below is a research priority list, not a buy ranking. First: PONS – The Shovel-Selling Logic

PONS is currently the most worthy asset for systematic research because it has at least verifiable business metrics:

With Robinhood's backing, and Robinhood's intention to continue this, stock tokens will evolve from "on-chain stock mirrors" into: quoted assets; collateral; lending assets; liquid assets; meme units of account; community treasury assets; and underlying assets for leveraged and structured products. This is a financial experiment with long-term value. The most valuable aspect is not the on-chain meme, but the monetization, collateralization, and composability of stock tokens. For this to truly impact the US stock market in the future, we need to see: a total supply of Stock Tokens increasing by tens or even hundreds of times; authorized participants continuously increasing their real stock inventory; hundreds of millions or even billions of dollars worth of Stock Tokens locked up in crypto-stock Memes and DeFi; a sufficiently small marginal trading volume of real stocks; and a consistently smooth issuance, redemption, and arbitrage mechanism. data.title: The History of Visa: How a Card Became a Global Payment Infrastructure
data.description:
In 2018, a software company I worked for became a Visa vendor. At that time, as a Visa vendor, we helped them with some innovative business in China. The company was in its third year, and we had already obtained various certifications such as High-Tech Enterprise and ISO. Visa was the first Fortune 500 company to become our supplier, and we felt pretty good about ourselves. From contacting Visa to completing the vendor registration process, it took us about six months. At that time, my understanding of Visa was simply that its logo was on our logo wall, and customers would think, "Wow, that's impressive." To me, it was a globally renowned fintech company, the weighty logo on credit cards, and the most prominent place on our logo wall. Around that time, WeChat Mini Programs were emerging, and the question we discussed with Visa's Indian technical team was: What is a WeChat Mini Program? We needed to explain to them that WeChat is not just a simple chat tool, but a local super platform encompassing payment, social networking, services, content, and transaction entry points. A WeChat Mini Program is not simply a mobile website; it's closer to a new way of distributing applications and providing services. Back then, we did localization for many foreign companies. Go Local sounds easy, but it's quite difficult in practice. It's not just about translating English into Chinese, changing a logo, connecting to a local payment interface, or opening a Chinese WeChat Official Account. True localization means entering a system that has already established its own rules, entry points, user habits, and business relationships. Last year, after starting to work in payments, I've come to understand more and more about the saying: "Money is local." While money appears to flow globally, its accounts, licenses, clearing, identity, risk, taxation, merchant relationships, and user habits all heavily rely on local systems. Back then, I saw Visa as a very strong Fortune 500 client; now, looking at the company from a different perspective—from the angles of payments, infrastructure, and cash flow—I'm beginning to realize that Visa's true capability isn't just issuing a card or owning a global brand. It's more like establishing a common transaction order between different banks, merchants, consumers, and countries. People see the Visa logo in shopping malls, hotels, airports, and e-commerce websites, and naturally assume it's a "credit card company." However, Visa doesn't define itself as a credit card company. On its website, it describes itself as "the world's leading digital payments company" and "a trusted payments network." Visa is not a bank; it doesn't issue cards directly to consumers, nor does it extend credit to them. Banks are responsible for issuing cards, managing accounts, and providing credit; acquiring institutions and payment service providers are responsible for serving merchants. Visa sits in between, responsible for enabling the identification, authorization, clearing, and settlement of payments between different institutions. Therefore, Visa's history deserves to be reinterpreted as a history of organization, power, and infrastructure. I. 1958: A Card and a Market That Didn't Yet Exist In 1958, Visa wasn't yet called Visa. At the time, it was simply a credit card business launched by Bank of America in California, called BankAmericard. Bank of America wasn't just addressing whether consumers needed to borrow money for purchases, but also whether merchants would accept this new payment method, and how banks would record transactions, manage credit, and handle fund transfers between different accounts. In other words, this product wasn't a one-sided market from the beginning. Without consumers, merchants wouldn't accept it; without merchants, consumers had no reason to hold it; without banks providing credit and accounts, the entire system couldn't function. Figure 1: Fresno Drop in 1958. First create the users, then create the use cases. Fresno Drop: Create Users First, Then Create Use Cases. In September 1958, Bank of America mailed BankAmericard cards to approximately 60,000 residents of Fresno, many of whom had not applied for the card beforehand. This operation later became known as the Fresno Drop. This is a market launch method that seems quite aggressive today. The bank didn't conduct a lengthy user education process first, nor did it wait for consumers to apply; instead, it directly delivered the credit cards to them. At the same time, Bank of America communicated with local merchants in advance, ensuring that these consumers had places to spend their cards. This wasn't about how many cards were mailed out at once; Bank of America did two things simultaneously: gave consumers a payment tool and prepared merchants to accept it. If you only send out cards without building a merchant acceptance network, consumers are just receiving a useless piece of plastic. If you only try to persuade merchants, but don't have enough consumers holding the cards, merchants have no reason to invest time and resources. This story seems very much like growth hacking; it doesn't even involve any special techniques. Bank of America did something very direct: put the cards in consumers' hands and then find merchants to accept them. However, because there wasn't a mature credit card market at the time, this direct action simultaneously undertook market education, user acquisition, merchant expansion, and risk testing. But often in business, this is probably the most realistic story. Many things that are later summarized as strategies, models, and flywheels often didn't start out so complicated. It might simply be someone knocking on a door first, finding a group of customers, and then gradually filling in the gaps on the other end. Just like the finest ingredients, they often only require the simplest cooking methods in the end. The real difficulty lies not in explaining concepts in a beautiful way, but in making the first real transactions. In one episode of our podcast discussing UnionPay's overseas expansion, we mentioned a similar sentiment: many global networks didn't begin in the grand way they seem today. They started by following tour groups, first serving a group of real people already moving across borders, and then gradually adding merchants, banks, and payment networks. This may not sound grand, but it might be the most authentic beginning of globalization.

Of course, Fresno Drop This also brought serious problems: fraud, bad debts, consumer complaints, and regulatory pressure. The practice of sending out large numbers of unsolicited credit cards was later banned. This was not a growth method to be emulated; it was more like a prototype experiment in the payments market: it proved that consumers and merchants could be simultaneously drawn into a new system, and it also exposed the risks and responsibilities that the credit card business had to face. The first phase of BankAmericard was proving that consumers and merchants were willing to use a new payment tool. The second phase was proving that this tool could not forever belong to only one bank. In 1966, Bank of America began licensing BankAmericard to other banks. For Bank of America, this was the fastest way to expand its network: other banks could bring their own customers, their own merchants, and their own local resources, while Bank of America... There's no need to rebuild branches in every city. But payment networks are different from ordinary franchises. If a restaurant licenses its brand to another, the two restaurants can operate relatively independently. Payment networks, however, require participants to jointly process the same transaction. A card issued by a Seattle bank might be used at a merchant in Los Angeles; a card issued by a Bank of America might be used in Japan. Different banks must exchange transaction information, complete fund clearing, and agree on who bears the losses from fraud, chargebacks, and operational errors. What was originally an internal business of a single bank has become a shared infrastructure among multiple banks. III. Dee Hock: When Competitors Must Jointly Build Networks Dee Hock, later known as the founder of Visa and its first CEO, was not originally from Bank of America. In 1966, he joined the National Bank of Commerce in Seattle. This was a local bank, but it was authorized by Bank of America to issue BankAmericard in the Pacific Northwest. Bank of America headquarters owned the BankAmericard brand and licensing system; National Bank of Commerce was the authorized bank that actually brought the card into local banking operations, issued it to customers, and integrated it into the merchant network. Dee Hock was on the latter side. In 1967, Hock began to oversee the bank's BankAmericard project. At that time, Visa had not yet been established, and Hock was not a corporate executive responsible for global strategy. He was simply a local bank manager handling a credit card business that had crossed banking boundaries. This allowed him to see some problems that Bank of America headquarters might not easily see. Headquarters saw BankAmericard expanding rapidly, with more and more banks willing to join. Hock, however, saw the chaos in the actual operation of this authorization system: how different banks exchanged transactions, who bore the responsibility for fraud and bad debts, how interbank payments were cleared, who should manage a system used by competing banks, and how the banks shared the system's construction costs. In other words, his initial challenge wasn't "how to sell more cards," but rather: how to transform a product belonging to one bank into a network used by many competing banks? This question later propelled Hock from a local bank to the core of Visa. In 1968, Hock... He participated in a committee composed of authorized banks, beginning to push BankAmericard from an authorized project of the Bank of America into an organization jointly managed by participating banks. At this point, participants were both partners and competitors: they needed to share a payment infrastructure, yet still competed on card issuance, customer and merchant relationships. In 1969, Hock organized a bankers' conference at the Alta Mira Hotel in Sausalito, California. The discussion wasn't about how to improve the business of any particular bank, but rather whether to jointly build a system that all banks would rely on: who would own the network, who would set the common rules, who would make decisions on behalf of the participants, and how to convince different banks that the organization wouldn't favor any one of them. Figure 2: Dee Hock convenes bankers to discuss how to allow competitors to share a single infrastructure. In 1970, BankAmericard separated from Bank of America to form the independent National BankAmericard Inc., jointly controlled by the participating banks. This step, seemingly a concession by Bank of America, was actually an exchange of scale. Bank of America relinquished direct control of the network in exchange for greater bank participation; other banks gained governance rights and accepted common rules; and the entire system gained greater neutrality. Visa traded partial ownership for the scale of the entire network. Visa's later organizational logic can be summarized as: competing on customer relationships and cooperating on infrastructure. This is an organizational approach later termed "chaordic" by Dee Hock: neither a hierarchical organization entirely controlled by a central authority, nor a free market without rules, but rather, under common rules, multiple competing participants jointly maintain a set of infrastructure. It doesn't solve the problem of "who wins all the business," but rather another: without a common network, no single bank can complete the business alone; but if the network is completely controlled by one bank, other banks have little incentive to join. Global infrastructure is often not designed by the headquarters of a single company, but rather is forced to be jointly organized when different participants can no longer solve problems independently. IV. Why Visa: A Brand Rebranding and a Power Shift By the 1970s, BankAmericard had entered multiple countries. However, banks in different markets used different names: Barclaycard in the UK, Chargex in Canada, and Sumitomo Card in Japan. A global network, but no globally unified identity. In 1976, BankAmericard changed its name to Visa. This name was selected through internal employee solicitation and screening, with key criteria including ease of pronunciation, easy recognition, and the ability to transcend language and cultural boundaries. The name `BankAmericard` belongs to the Bank of... America, with its distinctly American connotations, and Visa, on the other hand, does not belong to any single bank. The word "Visa" comes from French, further derived from Latin, originally meaning something close to "a document that has been seen or examined," later becoming a passport endorsement, a permit allowing entry into another country. From a branding perspective, it corresponds well with payment networks: Visa can be understood as a permit to enter a particular country, or as a pass to a global business network. For consumers, it means "I can pay here"; for banks and merchants, it means "I can access this network." Therefore, the 1976 name change accomplished three things simultaneously: organizationally separating it from the Bank of America... America, in the market, gained a name that could be spread globally, symbolically transforming from a single bank's credit card to a network logo used by multiple banks. V. VisaNet: Turning Payment Rules into Technological Infrastructure How can a transaction between different banks be completed in seconds? Early credit cards relied on paper, telephone, and manual processing. After a merchant swiped the card, staff might need to call the bank to confirm the credit limit. The bank would then determine if the card was valid, if the consumer had sufficient credit, and finally record the transaction. Back then, a payment was more like a series of phone calls requiring manual relay, rather than the instant results after a click as we see today. title="7507991" alt="xX02NKcbDH0EUUdGfTuyP8dhX5LRs0cIo7jZOd0O.png">

But as more and more banks issue BankAmericard and more and more merchants accept the card, manual processing quickly becomes a bottleneck. The larger the payment network, the more complex the relationships between transactions become.

data.title: Global bond market turmoil: Which asset classes will be affected?
data.description:
Recently, alarm bells have been ringing in global bond markets. From Washington to Tokyo, from London to Sydney, and then to Berlin and Paris—bond yields are collectively rising, reaching new highs. The yield on the 10-year US Treasury note rose to its highest level since January 2025; the yield on the 10-year Japanese government bond touched 3%, the first time since 1996; the yields on the 10-year Australian and German government bonds both rose to their highest levels since 2011; and the yield on the 10-year French government bond rose to its highest level since 2008. Rising bond yields correspond to falling bond prices. Several experts say that rising inflation risks and expectations of interest rate hikes are a major trigger. On the evening of August 28, Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh pointed out at the Jackson Hole Economic Symposium that inflation remains above the Fed's 2% target. Therefore, the Fed's primary focus should be on prices. Data from the CME Group's FedWatch Tool shows that as of the afternoon of September 3, the probability of a 25 basis point rate hike by the Fed in September was 60.2%, a significant increase from 35.4% a week earlier. "Currently, a surge in bond supply is flooding the market, while demand has not expanded accordingly. Investors demanding higher risk premiums is a normal market reaction," said Qu Qiang, Vice Dean of the Institute of Regional and Country Studies at Minzu University of China. He also believes that the simultaneous surge in yields on government bonds in the US, Japan, UK, Australia, Germany, France, and other countries is the result of a multi-faceted resonance of fiscal, monetary, geopolitical, and structural forces. The primary driver comes from fiscal pressures on major economies. Debt levels remain high. A report released by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) in March 2026 shows that outstanding sovereign debt of OECD countries reached a record high of $61 trillion in 2025, up from $55 trillion in 2024, marking the largest annual increase since the pandemic. Part of this increase comes from the pricing effect of the depreciating dollar, pushing up the dollar-denominated debt of non-US economies. Measured as a percentage of GDP, sovereign debt remained stable at 83% in 2024-2025, but is projected to climb to 85% in 2026, the highest level since 2021. Meanwhile, demand has shown signs of reduction. Core buying of US Treasuries is weakening; in the UK, demand for government bonds from long-term investors less sensitive to price changes has declined, and the Bank of England's support for the bond market is less than before. In the Eurozone, central banks' bond holdings have continued to decline, and the demand from stable, price-insensitive investors has narrowed. The Japanese bond market is experiencing a situation where central banks are reducing their holdings while life insurance companies are selling off their bonds. This reversal in supply and demand is reshaping the pricing logic of sovereign bonds. Qu Qiang stated that since 2023, yields on sovereign bonds from major developed economies have barely declined during global geopolitical conflicts. This means the market is beginning to price sovereign bonds based on "credit risk" rather than simply "interest rate risk," and higher term premiums will be embedded in the global financial system for a long time, potentially signaling the end of the low-interest-rate era. The risk-free nature of government bonds is being reassessed. Qu Qiang believes an important signal is that the risk-free asset attribute of government bonds is being reassessed by the market.

U.S. Treasury yields across all maturities surged at one point. On September 1, the yields on 2-year, 5-year, and 10-year U.S. Treasury bonds reached 4.39%, 4.55%, and 4.79%, respectively, all hitting their highest levels since January 2025. While ultra-long-term bonds saw slight fluctuations, they remained generally high; the yields on 20-year and 30-year U.S. Treasury bonds were both at 5.27% on September 1.

Just two weeks prior, on August 17th, both yields reached 5.3% and 5.31% respectively, setting new highs since October 2023 and June 2007. Across the Pacific, Japanese bond yields also repeatedly broke multi-year records. On September 1st, the yield on 2-year Japanese government bonds reached 1.802%, the highest since May 1995; the yield on 10-year government bonds was 2.987%, a new high since September 1996; and the yield on 20-year government bonds reached 3.859%, a new high since July 1996. The European market was not spared either. On September 1st, the yields on UK 2-year, 10-year, and 30-year government bonds were 4.61%, 5.26%, and 5.89% respectively, reaching new highs since February 2024, June 2008, and March 1998. Australian 2-year and 10-year yields were 4.83% and 5.19%, reaching new highs since June and July 2011 respectively. German 2-year, 10-year, and 30-year yields were 2.97%, 3.36%, and 3.84%, with the 2-year yield reaching a new high since June 2024, and the 10-year and 30-year yields both reaching new highs since April 2011. French 1-year and 10-year government bond yields were 2.944% and 4.203%, reaching new highs since September 2024 and November 2008 respectively. The rise in yields corresponds to a decline in bond prices. Professor Hu Jie of the Shanghai Advanced Institute of Finance at Shanghai Jiao Tong University and former senior economist at the Federal Reserve believes that the simultaneous rise in yields on government bonds in many countries, reaching relatively high levels, is primarily driven by the strong rise in US Treasury yields, which has been transmitted to global markets through a pricing anchor effect. Regarding US Treasury bonds themselves, this round of yield increases is driven by multiple factors: rising expectations of Fed rate hikes; increased US debt interest burdens leading to a weakening market assessment of its sovereign creditworthiness and pushing up risk premiums; and competition for funds from AI (artificial intelligence) related industries, whether funds flow into the stock market or real economy financing, creating competition for government bonds. Meanwhile, Hu Jie believes that the debt governance situation in many developed economies is not optimistic, and the market is becoming more cautious about their fiscal sustainability and sovereign creditworthiness risks, further pushing up government bond risk premiums. Against the backdrop of rising global debt, demand in the bond market has shown signs of weakening. Core buying of US Treasuries has weakened. Data from the US Treasury shows that from January to June 2026, major US Treasury holders collectively increased their holdings by $7.7 billion, the lowest increase for the same period since 2023. Japan and China, however, reduced their holdings by $108.6 billion and $61.9 billion respectively, the largest reductions for the same period since 2001 and 2022. Turning to the UK market, the Bank of England's July 2026 Financial Stability Report shows a decline in demand for UK government bonds from long-term investors with lower price sensitivity, such as defined benefit pension funds. At the same time, the Bank of England's support for the bond market has decreased. A report released by the Bank of England on August 4, 2026, showed that the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) voted to further reduce the stock of UK government bonds held through the Asset Purchase Facility (APF) by £70 billion between October 2025 and September 2026. The APF is the core tool of the Bank of England's quantitative easing program. Regarding the Eurozone, according to the 2026 Eurozone Stability Watch report released in July 2026, the demand for stable and price-insensitive allocations in the Eurozone bond market has narrowed in recent years; over the past five years, the proportion of sovereign bonds held by insurance companies in their total investment assets has fallen from 26% to 20%. Central bank-level support for the bond market has also weakened. In a speech in June 2025, ECB Executive Board member Philip R. Lane mentioned that the Eurozone central bank system's share of the Eurozone government bond market had fallen from a peak of 33% at the end of 2022 to 25% in the first quarter of 2025. Looking at the Japanese market, Qu Qiang believes that the Japanese government bond market is moving away from the "central bank + life insurance" dual-pillar holding model, exhibiting a pattern of central bank reductions and life insurance institutions selling off their holdings. The Public Pension Investment Fund (GPIF) of Japan can only absorb limited supply pressure. The Bank of Japan, as the largest holder of Japanese government bonds, continues to reduce its holdings. The Bank of Japan's "Flow of Funds Statement for the First Quarter of 2026" released in June 2026 shows that in the first quarter of 2026, compared to the fourth quarter of 2025, the Bank of Japan, which accounts for over 42% of the total outstanding government long-term and short-term debt, reduced its holdings by 17.6 trillion yen. The Bank of Japan's August 2026 report also shows that from the end of June 2024 to the end of March 2026, insurance institutions' holdings of Japanese government bonds decreased by a total of 5 trillion yen. What will be the impact on financial assets? The continued rise in global bond yields has rapidly spread, triggering a chain reaction of repricing across various global assets. The equity market, after initially facing pressure, has rebounded. From August 27 to September 1, major US stock indices generally retreated, with the S&P 500 falling over 1.28%, the Nasdaq Composite falling over 1.66%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average falling over 1.49%, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, with stronger growth potential, plummeting over 4.9%. From September 1 to September 3, the S&P 500 rose over 1.52%, the Nasdaq rose over 1.85%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose over 1.74%, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index rose slightly by 0.56%. Hu Jie's analysis points out that the real yield on government bonds is the risk-free benchmark for global asset pricing, and changes in benchmark interest rates will lead to a revaluation of almost all financial assets. For the equity market, high-valuation growth sectors such as technology, AI, and innovative drugs are highly sensitive to the risk-free discount rate. Rising long-term yields directly increase the cost of asset discounting, compressing the valuation space of growth stocks. External liquidity tightening pressure also spread to emerging and mature stock markets globally. From early August to September 3, many regional stock indices experienced significant adjustments: the Hang Seng Tech Index fell by more than 9.4% cumulatively from August 5 to September 3; the Korea Composite Stock Price Index (KOSPI) fell by more than 5.7% from August 14 to September 3; the Nikkei 225 Index fell by more than 7% from August 17 to September 3; and the CSI 300 Index corrected by about 4% during the same period. The gold market also experienced periodic fluctuations. Under pressure from rising real interest rates, gold prices fell in the short term. From August 24 to September 3, spot gold fell more than 4.2% against the US dollar. Gu Fengda, chief analyst at Guoxin Futures, stated that the core reason for the gold price correction from late August to early September was the short-term tightening of liquidity caused by the systemic repricing of the global bond market. However, this decline is only a temporary market correction and does not signify the end of the long-term bull market for gold. In his view, in the medium to long term, the sharp adjustments in overseas bond markets and the exposure of high global debt risks are continuously eroding the dollar's credit system, further solidifying the medium- to long-term allocation value of safe-haven assets represented by gold. In the foreign exchange market, rising US Treasury yields initially supported a stronger dollar. Wind data shows that from August 19 to September 1, the dollar index rose by more than 0.87%. From September 1 to September 3, the dollar index fell by more than 0.66%. Major non-US currencies weakened slightly at one point. Among them, the euro depreciated by more than 0.45% against the US dollar from August 20 to September 3; the pound sterling depreciated by more than 0.9% against the US dollar from August 25 to September 3; the yen fluctuated sharply, weakening against the US dollar by more than 1.89% from August 3 to September 1. From September 1 to September 3, the yen appreciated by more than 2.7% against the US dollar. The RMB exchange rate has maintained an appreciation trend for a considerable period. From April 9, 2025 to September 3, 2026, the offshore RMB exchange rate against the US dollar has appreciated by nearly 9%, while the onshore RMB exchange rate against the US dollar has appreciated by more than 8.5%. While bond yields in many countries and regions around the world have continued to rise, Chinese government bond yields have continued to decline. Wind data shows that the yield on China's 10-year government bonds has fluctuated and fallen from a high of 4.0518% in January 2018 to 1.6811% on September 3, 2026. Currently, the spread between the 10-year Chinese and US government bond yields is nearly 310 basis points. Hu Jie stated that although the existence of the interest rate differential will put some downward pressure on the RMB exchange rate, the most prominent influencing factor on the current China-US exchange rate is the trade surplus, and the existence of the trade surplus will drive the RMB to appreciate. Data from China's Ministry of Commerce shows that from January to July 2026, China's trade surplus with the US will be approximately US$170.8 billion, an increase compared to approximately US$165.521 billion in the same period of 2025. From August 31 to September 1, 2026, Pan Gongsheng, Governor of the People's Bank of China (PBOC), stated at the G20 Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors Meeting that China never deliberately pursues a trade surplus. The PBOC will continue to promote the transformation of its monetary policy framework, improve its interest rate system, and continue to implement a moderately loose monetary policy.

data.title: Shenyu: Knowledge and Practice in the AI ​​Era
data.description: Recently, Shenyu, co-founder of Cobo, and Jinming, founder of Jilian Technology, had an in-depth conversation, covering topics ranging from investment systems, Bitcoin, DeFi, and AI agents to the meaning of life. During the conversation, Shenyu shed his early "mining giant" aura, displaying a highly rational self-reflection, frankly admitting that his early success had an element of luck, and reflecting on his cognitive leap of viewing DeFi as a "condensed history of 200 years of finance." In an era where AI is deeply taking over cognitive input, this cutting-edge Builder remains committed to long-termism, maintaining a clear and unique independent mindset in the volatile crypto world. The following are the core observations and key takeaways from this dialogue: "DeFi is a compressed course in financial history." Shenyu views DeFi as an experimental field for understanding finance. Mechanisms such as lending, market making, and liquidity mining are essentially re-answering questions that traditional finance has already addressed. Personally participating in the protocols is equivalent to experiencing hundreds of years of financial product evolution in a very short time. For him, the value of DeFi thus motivates him to brush up on his financial history and theoretical knowledge. Therefore, his investment framework grew from practice. Shenyu mentioned that he didn't have a complete investment framework in his early days; his later method was closer to a cycle: first practice, accumulating experience in the real market, then abstracting patterns from the results to form a framework, and finally training it into intuition. The key is to constantly raise questions in action, and then supplement financial history and theory in reverse. "After AI lowers execution costs, human will becomes even more important." AI is significantly shortening the distance from idea to implementation. In the past, the main obstacle to many ideas was the high cost of execution; now, knowledge, tools, and action capabilities are concentrated in the hands of individuals. With a sufficiently clear "seed," it can be quickly tested. The more advanced the technology, the more important a person's sense of direction, judgment, and will to act persistently become. But increased possibilities also amplify the Builder's confusion. AI brings almost limitless executable space, making "topic selection" the biggest challenge. Shenyu frankly admits that he once had a strong sense of mission and creative impulse during the mining era, but now he is in a more confused phase, not yet finding a sufficiently large and systematic direction. However, he still defines himself as a Builder: one of the meanings of his existence is to add more possibilities to the world that didn't exist before. "Agents are evolving from efficiency tools into external brains for cognition and self-understanding." Shenyu has deeply embedded AI and Agents into his daily life. On the information input side, the tasks of reading original long articles, filtering materials, and compressing them into PPTs are completed by a note-taking system based on evolutionary thinking and AI-filtered daily reports. For daily interaction and cognitive assistance, he has configured three Agents, each with a specific role: one is a tool-rational Agent, providing highly rational action plans and decision-making suggestions; another is a more feminine, gentle Agent, responsible for emotion analysis and empathy, and even astutely pointed out that he "might have death anxiety"; and the third is a blind spot alert Agent, which, based on his historical information and personal behavior, specifically helps him identify cognitive blind spots. The role of the agent has transcended that of a traditional assistant, evolving into a companion-type "cognitive external brain." It not only processes information and tasks for people but also deeply participates in emotional care, blind spot correction, and the construction of a second thinking system. "Core assets must first have sufficiently large long-term value potential." In the interview, Shenyu also revealed his first principle for selecting core assets: the TAM (Total Asset Management) must be large enough, and there must be a macro-level vision behind it that supports long-term holding. He believes that only when an asset not only has short-term opportunities but also has the potential to participate in shaping the technological, financial, or social structures of the next decade or even longer is it worth considering for a core holding. He employs a three-tiered position management logic: first, a small initial position for discovery; then, increasing the allocation through continuous verification; and finally, entering the core phase after clearly understanding the long-term vision, where the position may increase to approximately 20%. Currently, only Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Tesla have truly passed this test; SpaceX is still in the observation and timing phase. Whether Ethereum can remain in the core position depends on the next round of infrastructure value. Although Ethereum has entered his core asset list, its status is being reassessed. The new criterion is whether Ethereum can further become the operational and collaborative infrastructure for AI Agents. If it can meet the new demands of the machine economy, Ethereum may maintain its core status; otherwise, the original investment logic needs to be re-evaluated. The fundamental difference between gold and Bitcoin lies in the clash between two paradigms and camps: the "digital currency + AI" camp versus the "gold + industrial manufacturing" camp. Shenyu believes "Bitcoin is better gold" primarily because of its complete lack of intermediaries and the empowerment it grants sovereign individuals control over their assets. Traditional gold often requires layers of intermediaries and institutional custody to establish ownership and liquidity, while Bitcoin allows individuals complete control and disposal without relying on any intermediaries, truly realizing individual asset sovereignty. There are two types of technologies that significantly enhance the capabilities of sovereign individuals. Bitcoin (BTC) changes how individuals control and dispose of their assets, allowing value to be held and transferred autonomously, independent of traditional institutions; AI, on the other hand, enhances the boundaries of individual capabilities, enabling individuals to complete knowledge and execution tasks that previously required organization. The former strengthens asset sovereignty, while the latter amplifies individual productivity. Traditional asset allocation emphasizes reducing portfolio volatility through low-correlation assets such as gold, stocks, and Bitcoin, but Shenyu does not agree with this investment philosophy. "Human cognition and energy are limited; the assets one can truly understand in depth are actually very few." Rather than buying gold that one doesn't understand just to satisfy asset allocation theories, Shenyu's investment philosophy leans more towards "less is more." He believes that defensive capabilities don't come from holding more asset classes, because correlations tend to converge in extreme situations. In a true systemic crisis (an extreme case), those assets you thought were mutually restraining often end up collapsing simultaneously or behaving in unison. Diversification is effective in extremely stable markets, but it often fails in the face of real "disasters."
